heading: The American years, out of the records at last
lead: For a year this archive has known the Eleven only from a chart their cousins printed in 2012 — birth dates from a cassette tape and a bundle of handwritten notes, and a compiler who said plainly there would be errors. On 9 September 2026 David took a subscription to Findmypast and gave it an hour. What came back is the family's American half in documents: a census household with three of them in one Brooklyn flat, two marriage licences, a draft card, a war grave and a death date.
note: Children born after 1926 who may still be living are counted here but not named, in keeping with this site's rule. Their years are given because the years are the evidence.

rows.lab: Brooklyn, 1 April 1930 — three of the Eleven under one roof
rows.text:
United States Census of 1930, Brooklyn, Kings County, New York — NARA T626, roll 1495.

Read the four names against the reunion chart. **Albina** is the sixth of the Eleven, born at Gračišće on 14 April 1900. **Anthony** is the eldest, born 18 February 1887 — and the census gives his year of immigration as **1922**, which is the year of the passenger list this archive found under his name. And «**Grochina**» is what a Brooklyn enumerator made of **Gioacchino**, the tenth child, born 12 August 1907, whom the family called **Bruno**.

**A sister, her husband, and two of her brothers, in one flat, on one census night.** One of them had crossed the Atlantic eight years earlier; one would marry a German girl from Hanover sixteen months later. Nothing in this archive had put any two of them in the same room.

rows.lab: «Gallignana» returns ten records in the whole of Findmypast — and three are ours
rows.text:
The obvious search, and nobody had run it. Type the village's Italian name into the keyword box of a database of billions of records and **ten results come back**. Three carry this family's name.

**Joseph Defranceschi — Petition for naturalization, Brooklyn, 1915.** «Birth date **12 Mar 1892** · Birth country Austria · **Birth place as transcribed: Gallignana, Austria**.» Petition 13838, declaration 22660, **certificate 1104860**.

**Albina Schinkepan — Petition for naturalization, Brooklyn, 1928.** «Birth date **14 Apr 1900** · **Birth place as transcribed: Gallignana, Austria** · Husband **Frank Schinkepan, born 24 Feb 1896**.» Petition 100185.

**The name of this village is written into the federal records of the United States, twice, by two of the eleven children of Antonio and Maria.** Not «Austria», not «Italy», not «Trieste» — *Gallignana*. It is the plainest documentary tie between the hill town this archive is built on and the country half the family went to.

The other seven are the village's other emigrants, and they are worth naming because a village of that size sends its people out together: **Poldrugovac** Thomas (b.1899, petitions of 1921 and 1941) and **Poldrugovaz** Santo (b.1900, 1946); **Millassich** Leopoldo (b.1883) and Emilia (b.1889), arriving 1912; **Lanza** Anthony (b.1892); **Silich** Victor. Six surnames out of one parish, in the New York courts.

rows.lab: 11 … 1922 · the Conte Rosso, Genoa to New York
rows.text:
And then the two records that sit beside each other in the index, one number apart, on one page of one ship's manifest.

**«Antonio De Franceschi · Passenger · Male · Age 35y · Birth year 1887 · Nationality Italy, Slovenian · Residence G. Pedena, Venezia, Italy · Year 1922 · Departure port Genoa · Arrival New York · Ship name Conte Rosso.»** And in the relations field: «**Departure port relation (WIFE): Marta Defranceschi**».

**«Albina De Franceschi · Passenger · Female · Age 22y · Birth year 1900 · Nationality Italy, Italian · Residence G. Gallignana, Venezia · Year 1922 · Departure port Genoa · Arrival New York · Ship name Conte Rosso.»**

**Brother and sister, thirty-five and twenty-two, on the same crossing.** The eldest of the Eleven and the sixth, going down to Genoa from opposite ends of the same few miles of Istria — he from **Pedena, which is Pićan**, the cathedral town over the hill; she from **Gallignana**. The *Conte Rosso* was a Lloyd Sabaudo liner two years old that year.

Three details this archive did not have and would not have guessed. **Antonio was living at Pićan, not Gračišće.** **He left a wife behind him** — Marta Defranceschi, named at the departure port, which is why the census of 1930 finds him married but lodging with his sister eight years later. And an American clerk wrote his nationality as «**Italy, Slovenian**» and hers as «Italy, Italian» — the same household, the same village, sorted into two nations by a man at a desk in New York harbour.

Albina's husband takes a different spelling in every record — **Chinikopan** on the 1925 marriage licence, **Chinkojan** in the 1930 census, **Schinkepan** on her 1928 petition. Search the keyword **Pisino** and he appears under a fourth: **«Schinkopan, Frank, born 1896 — United States Naturalization Petitions, New York, 1920 and 1926.»**

Born **24 February 1896**, out of **Pisino — Pazin**, the county town. He declared his intention in 1920, petitioned in 1926, married Albina of Gallignana in between, and by 1930 was keeping a Brooklyn household with two of her brothers in it.

Four spellings of one man, and the archive can now say where he came from.

rows.lab: 23 April 1925 — Albina's marriage, and her mother's name
rows.text:
**Albine Defranceschi**, spinster, aged 25, born 1900 — married **Frank Chinikopan**, aged 28, born 1897, at **Kings County, New York, on 23 April 1925**.

«**Father's first name(s): Anton. Mother's first name(s): Maria. Mother's last name: Volhart.**»

That is the couple at the head of the 2012 chart — *Antonio DeFranceschi 1856–1924 + Maria Valhart 1867–1945* — and it is the surname the Gračišće **Status Animarum** of 1925 spells **Volhardt**. A New York clerk, working from what the bride told him, wrote her mother's maiden name into the civil record of the State of New York.

The reunion album's «Albina Chinkopan» is **Frank Chinikopan**, and this archive now has the day.

rows.lab: 30 July 1931 — Bruno's marriage, and the name the gravestone cut off
rows.text:
**Bruno De Franceschi**, single, aged 24, **birth place: Istria, Italy** — married **Gerda Seedorf**, aged 18, **birth place: Hanover, Germany**, at **Manhattan on 30 July 1931**.

His father **Anton**; his mother **Mary Walhal**. Her father John Seedorf; her mother Anna Huntsen.

The stone at Nine Partners Cemetery, Millbrook, gave this archive a wife it could read only as «**Gerda Se…**». She was **Gerda Seedorf of Hanover**, eighteen years old, marrying a boy from Istria in Manhattan two years into the Depression.

rows.lab: 1939 — Bruno swears out his declaration of intention
rows.text:
**United States Naturalization Petitions, Brooklyn, Kings, New York, 1939.** Declaration of intention no. **284221**; certificate **2-665402**.

«First name Bruno · Last name De Franceschi · **Birth date 12 Aug 1907** · Spouse **Gerda de Franceschi, born 15 Jan 1913** · **Relation 2: child, born 2 December 1932**.»

**12 August 1907** is the reunion album's date for Gioacchino, to the day. Gerda petitioned in the same year; Bruno filed again in **1942**, indexed under both names as «Bruno de Franceschi **Or Seedorf**», and Gerda again in **1944**. There is a son, born 2 December 1932, who is not named here because he may be living.

rows.lab: Uncle Joe, from a draft card to a war grave
rows.text:
The second son, **Giuseppe — «Uncle Joe» — born 3 March 1892** on the chart. Four records, in order:

**1917–18 · World War I Draft Registration Cards, New York City board no. 27.** «Joseph Defranceschi · **Birth date 12 Mar 1892** · Place of birth as transcribed **Frieste** · Birth country **Austria** · Citizenship **United States**.» The American records this archive already had gave 12 March, not the chart's 3 March; the draft card is where that comes from. **Frieste** is Trieste — what an Istrian says to a New York clerk who has never heard of Gallignana.

**20 May 1926 · Manhattan.** He marries **Maria Duda**, born 1903 in New Jersey. «Father **Anton**; mother **Maria Valbart**.» The mother's name again, from a third child, in a third record.

**1 April 1940 · United States Census, Brooklyn.** Head of household, aged 48, born Austria, at the same address as in 1935. With him his wife **Mary**, 36, born New Jersey — Maria Duda — and **two children, a daughter born 1927 and a son born 1929**, both born in New Jersey. This archive had not known he had children.

**26 April 1940 · U.S. Veteran's Gravesites.** «Joseph De Franceschi · died 26 Apr 1940 · **Rank Sergeant · US Army · World War I** · **Long Island National Cemetery**, Farmingdale, New York · **Section F, Site 2918**.»

**Twenty-five days after the census taker wrote him down.** The grave record carries no birth year, so the identification rests on the name, the borough, and a First World War service that matches his own 1917 registration in New York City. This archive calls that strong and not proved — and notes that a man who registered for the American draft in 1917 as an Austrian-born citizen was, four months earlier, technically a subject of the empire his new country had just gone to war against.

The youngest of the Eleven, **Basilio, born 29 September 1909**. The Social Security Death Index and the obituary index agree: «**Basilio Defranceschi · 29 September 1909 – 15 June 1994 · New York, New York**», Social Security number issued in New York.

Born at Gračišće while it was Austria; died in New York City, aged eighty-four, in the summer of 1994. **This archive had no death date for him at all.**

rows.lab: The mother's name, in three hands
rows.text:
It is worth setting these side by side, because they were written by three different clerks, in three different years, from what three different children of the same woman told them:

· Albina, 1925 — «Anton · Maria **Volhart**»
· Joseph, 1926 — «Anton · Maria **Valbart**»
· Bruno, 1931 — «Anton · Mary **Walhal**»

And the parish book of souls at Gračišće, house 24: **Maria Volhardt**, 6 April 1867 – 3 October 1945.

Four spellings, one woman. This is what a German surname does in the mouths of Istrian children and the ears of New York registrars, and it is the strongest identification in this whole sweep: **the three of the Eleven who married in New York all named the same mother.**

fused.heading: And the family's own spelling turns up thirty-six times
fused.lead: «Defranceski» — fused, no particle, the way this family writes it — returns thirty-six records of its own. They are not Italian. They are Croatian, and they are post-war.

rows.lab: Philadelphia, 1954: five of them off one ship
rows.text:
**Josip Defranceski, 39, born 1915**, arrives at **Philadelphia in 1954 aboard the *Slovenija*** — a Jugolinija liner out of **Rijeka**. On the same lists: **Bosiljka, born 1918**, and three children born **1942, 1946 and 1947**, not named here because they may be living.

A man, his wife and three children, leaving Yugoslavia for America in 1954, sailing from the port this family's own line lived beside. Nothing connects them to it. The spelling does what no index can: it says these people wrote their name exactly as David's family does.

rows.lab: Horsham, Victoria — a Defranceski grave in Australia
rows.text:
**Zdravko Defranceski, 1922–1980**, died at **Horsham, Victoria**, aged 58. The Victorian death register names his parents: «Father **Anton**. Mother **Ursula**.» **Ruža «Rosa» Defranceski** died at Horsham on **30 January 1996**, occupation «home duties»; probate was granted on 6 May 1996. Both are in the Billion Graves index for Horsham cemetery.

The fused Croatian spelling, a father called Anton, and a grave in country Victoria — in the country this family's own line ends up in. **It is not a link and this page will not make it one.** It is the closest thing to one that a name-search has ever produced, and it can be tested: the Victorian death certificate will give Zdravko's birthplace.

rows.lab: The rest of the fused thirty-six
rows.text: **John J Defranceski, born 1917 — United States Army enlistment, Second World War.** **Giovanni Defranceski, born 1871 — married at Manhattan in 1894.** **Luigi Defranceski — married at Luzerne, Pennsylvania, in 1904.** **Petro Defranceski — a passenger list of 1912.** Nothing joins any of them to this line, and the living British and Australian entries in the same index are deliberately left out of this page.

honest: **What has changed and what has not.** Every fact above is a transcript read on a paid subscription, not an index guess — and the identifications rest on three independent things agreeing: a birth date already held from the parish book, a mother's maiden name already held from the book of souls, and a place. Where only a name and a place agree, this page says so. The images behind these transcripts have not been opened, and the images will carry more: the census sheets give street addresses, occupations and rents; the marriage licences give witnesses; the naturalisation file gives the ship and the date of arrival. **That is the next hour's work, not this one's.**
source: Findmypast, full subscription, 9 September 2026 — United States Census 1930 and 1940; United States Marriages (FamilySearch index); United States Naturalization Petitions; World War I Draft Registration Cards; U.S. Veteran's Gravesites; Social Security Death Index; United States Obituary Notices; Victoria Civil Deaths & Burials; Victoria Wills & Probate; Pennsylvania, Philadelphia Passenger Lists. Plus keyword searches on the place-names Gallignana, Pedena and Pisino. Transcripts only; no images opened.
